en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on Ants.
10. The Question of the Elephant’s Limbs “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you say—that ‘five limbs of the elephant should be taken’—which are those five limbs that should be taken?
“Just as, Great King, an elephant, while walking, tears up the earth;”
In the same way, Great King, a yogi practicing yoga must shatter all defilements by thoroughly scrutinizing the body.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the elephant that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, an elephant looks with its entire body; it gazes straight ahead and does not look about in various directions.

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga must look ahead with his entire body; he should not look to the cardinal or intermediate directions, nor gaze upward, nor look downward; he should keep his eyes fixed on the distance of a yoke’s length.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the elephant that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, an elephant does not sleep in a fixed place; having gone out to forage, it does not return to that same spot to dwell, nor does it have a permanent resting place.
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga, a follower of the spiritual life, should not have a fixed dwelling;

he should go for alms without a home. If a practitioner of insight sees a pleasant, suitable, and delightful place—a pavilion, the foot of a tree, a cave, or a mountain cleft—he should take up residence right there, but he should not make it his permanent, settled abode.
This, O Great King, is the third quality of the elephant that should be adopted.

Furthermore, O Great King, after an elephant has plunged into water, it plunges into a vast lotus lake filled with pure, stainless, cool water and covered with white, blue, red, and pink lotuses, where it sports the sport of a noble elephant;
even so, O Great King, by a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, [should one plunge] into that which is filled with the excellent waters of the Dhamma—pure, stainless, serene, and undisturbed.
Having plunged into the lotus pond of the Great Foundations of Mindfulness, which is strewn with the flowers of liberation, one should shake off and blow away all conditioned formations with wisdom;
thus should the play of the practitioner be played.
This, O Great King, is the fourth quality to be adopted from the elephant.
Furthermore, Great King, an elephant lifts its foot mindfully and places its foot down mindfully;
even so, Great King, a practitioner of yoga, being mindful and clearly comprehending,
should lift his foot mindfully and place his foot down mindfully— in every instance, whether advancing or retreating, or contracting or extending his limbs.
"One must be mindful and clearly comprehending.
This, Great King, is the fifth quality of an elephant that should be adopted.
And this, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God above gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:"
“Restraint with the body is good;
restraint with speech is good;
restraint with the mind is good.”
“Excellent is restraint in all things;
one who is restrained in all things and possesses a sense of shame is called ‘guarded.’”
The tenth question: On the Elephant’s Footprint.
The fourth chapter: On the Ants.
Its summary verse:
The termite, the cat, the rat, and the scorpion;
the mongoose, the jackal, and the deer.
A boar in the form of a cow is struck by an elephant.
